chapters.caption: Radcliffe Square — the cobbled heart of the university, with the Radcliffe Camera at its centre.
chapters.directions: From Radcliffe Square, walk north through the great gate on Catte Street into the Old Schools Quadrangle.
chapters.text: Start here, in Radcliffe Square, and just turn slowly in a circle. This cobbled square is the closest thing Oxford has to a town centre for the mind. Every building around you belongs to the university, and together they tell its whole story. To the south rises the spire of the University Church of St Mary the Virgin, where the university itself began. To the north is the Old Bodleian Library, the working heart of the whole system. East and west are the colleges of All Souls and Brasenose. And in the middle, like a great stone wedding cake, stands the round Radcliffe Camera, a reading room from 1749 and probably the most photographed building in Oxford. The square wasn't always this serene. Before the Camera was built, this was a jumble of houses, gardens and even a brewery, cleared away in the 1730s. What replaced them is a deliberate stage set for scholarship. Notice how quiet it is: no cars, just bicycles, students cutting through on their way to lectures, and readers hurrying to their desks. In a moment we'll step through the gate into the Old Schools Quadrangle, the courtyard behind the Bodleian's east front. But first, enjoy the view — generations of students have crossed this square with their heads in a book, and quite a few have walked straight into each other doing it.
chapters.title: Welcome to Radcliffe Square

chapters.caption: The Old Schools Quadrangle, built 1613–1624, with the Tower of the Five Orders in the centre.
chapters.directions: Cross the quadrangle to the Proscholium entrance on the south side, which leads into the Divinity School.
chapters.text: You're now standing in the Old Schools Quadrangle, the courtyard Sir Thomas Bodley built between 1613 and the 1620s to give his refounded library a proper home. Look at the doorways around you. Above each one, carved in Latin, is the name of a 'school' — the university's word for a subject. Logic, grammar, rhetoric, astronomy, music, medicine, law: this quadrangle was a whole university in one courtyard, with lecture and examination rooms stacked on every side, built to replace what Bodley grumpily called 'those ruinous little rooms' that stood here before. Now look up at the tower in the middle of the east side, the Tower of the Five Orders. It's a architecture lesson in itself: five storeys, each decorated with a different classical order of columns — Tuscan, Doric, Ionic, Corinthian and Composite — rising from plain to fancy like a student progressing through a degree. At the top sits a statue of James I, who was on the throne when this was built. Beneath your feet and all around you, this complex now holds millions of books — the Bodleian is one of Britain's copyright deposit libraries, entitled to a copy of everything published in the UK, and it grows by thousands of volumes every week. The entrance to the Divinity School is through the arched doorway called the Proscholium, on the south side of the quad. That's where we're headed next.
chapters.title: The Old Schools Quadrangle

chapters.caption: The Divinity School (1424–1488) — the university's oldest teaching room and first examination school.
chapters.directions: Stay in the Divinity School — the next chapter is all about the ceiling above you.
chapters.text: Take a breath as you walk in, because this room tends to stop conversations mid-sentence. The Divinity School was built between 1424 and 1488, and it is the university's oldest surviving teaching room — and its first purpose-built examination school. For centuries, this is where Oxford's theology students came to be taught and, more terrifyingly, to be examined. Examinations then were oral and public: a student would stand and defend a thesis in Latin, arguing a point of theology back and forth with his examiners, in front of anyone who cared to watch. Imagine doing your finals as a spectator sport, in a dead language, under this ceiling. The room is a single, glorious stone hall in the late Gothic style — long, low and cool, with tall windows that fill it with soft light. At one end, look for the raised stone pulpit from which lectures were delivered, and the rows where examiners sat. Despite the name, this wasn't a church; it was a working academic room, the ancestor of every lecture hall and exam room in the university. It still hosts ceremonies, concerts and events today, which is why it sometimes closes to visitors at short notice. Before you do anything else, though, do what everyone does. Stop, and look up.
chapters.title: The Divinity School: Oxford's Oldest Classroom

chapters.caption: The lierne vault, designed by William Orchard in the 1480s, carries 455 carved bosses.
chapters.directions: If you're on a guided tour, your guide will lead you upstairs to Duke Humfrey's Library next; self-guided visitors can admire it through this chapter, then head for the Weston Library.
chapters.text: The ceiling is the real masterpiece here. Designed by the master mason William Orchard in the 1480s, it's a lierne vault — a web of stone ribs that sprout extra decorative ribs, called liernes, which tie the whole surface into a pattern of stars and nets. Where the ribs meet, they're pinned by carved bosses: 455 of them, an entire stone menagerie and honour roll crammed overhead. Get your eye in and you'll pick out coats of arms of the university's benefactors, saints, bishops, angels, green men, animals and grotesques — each one a small thank-you note or signature in stone, because donors and masons liked to be remembered. The vault seems to float, and that's the trick of it: the real structural work is hidden, so the ceiling reads as lace rather than engineering. Now, the detail half the room has come for: film fans will recognise this hall as the Hogwarts infirmary in the Harry Potter films, where more than one young wizard woke up in a bed after a Quidditch mishap. It has also appeared in other films and television dramas — few rooms in England photograph this well. If you're on a self-guided ticket, you may only have about fifteen minutes in here, so spend them wisely: walk the full length once, slowly, then stand at the far end and look back for the classic postcard view down the hall.
chapters.title: Look Up: 455 Bosses and a Film Set

chapters.caption: Duke Humfrey's Library (opened 1488), the Bodleian's oldest reading room, sits directly above the Divinity School.
chapters.directions: After the Old Library, exit to Broad Street and cross over to the Weston Library, the modern building opposite the Sheldonian Theatre.
chapters.text: Directly above the Divinity School — reached on guided tours only — is the room that started it all: Duke Humfrey's Library, opened in 1488. Humfrey, Duke of Gloucester, younger brother of Henry V, gave the university more than 281 manuscripts, a gift so magnificent that Oxford built this room over its brand-new Divinity School to house it. It remains the oldest reading room in the Bodleian. The first thing to notice is the ceiling: not stone this time, but painted wooden panels, each bearing the arms of the university. Then look along the rows of book presses. When Sir Thomas Bodley refounded the library in 1602, after the collection had been scattered in the Reformation, books were so valuable that they were chained to the shelves — look for the lecterns and imagine every volume tethered by a chain long enough to read at the desk, but not to walk off with. Readers still work here today, in near silence, at the same desks, which is why tours keep voices low and cameras away; this is a library first and a sight second. Look, too, for the special reading booth built for King Charles I. On the longer tours you'll also pass through two more 17th-century rooms downstairs: Convocation House, where the university's parliament met and Charles I's own parliament sat during the Civil War, and the Chancellor's Court, complete with its oak dock, where students were tried for their misdemeanours. High jinks, formally punished — some things about student life never change.
chapters.title: Duke Humfrey's Library: Where the Books Were Chained

chapters.caption: Blackwell Hall, the Weston Library's light-filled public atrium, named for the famous Oxford bookshop.
chapters.directions: When you've finished in the Weston, exit onto Broad Street; the Sheldonian Theatre and the History of Science Museum are moments away, and Radcliffe Square is just around the corner.
chapters.text: Cross Broad Street and step into a completely different century. The Weston Library opened in 1940 as the New Bodleian, designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott — the architect who also gave Britain the red telephone box — and was beautifully rebuilt and reopened in 2015 as the home of the Bodleian's special collections: the rarest books, manuscripts, maps and archives. You enter into Blackwell Hall, a soaring, light-filled atrium named after the great Oxford bookshop across the road. Look up at the 'floating' book stacks seemingly suspended above the hall, and take a moment in the café — this is the relaxed, public face of a very serious research library. The headline act is the Treasures gallery, and it is genuinely treasurable. The displays rotate, but the cast of characters is reliably staggering: medieval illuminated manuscripts glowing with gold leaf, a Shakespeare folio, original drafts and letters by writers from Tolkien and Kafka to Jane Austen, early printed books, maps and scientific instruments — the working papers of civilisation, in glass cases, free to look at. A second gallery hosts changing exhibitions drawn from the same bottomless collections, so no two visits are alike. Give the Treasures at least twenty unhurried minutes, and read the labels: the stories of how these objects survived — through fires, wars, damp and indifference — are as gripping as the objects themselves.
chapters.title: The Weston Library: Blackwell Hall and the Treasures

chapters.caption: Convocation House, added in the 1630s, where the university's governing body met for over 300 years.
chapters.directions: Head south into Radcliffe Square for the University Church of St Mary the Virgin, the natural next stop.
chapters.text: Let's end back outside, with one last look at the whole picture. What you've seen today is really one organism in three bodies: a medieval schoolroom where students argued theology aloud, a chained library where books were treated like crown jewels, and a 21st-century vault where those same treasures are conserved, digitised and — in the Weston's free galleries — finally shown to anyone who walks in. The Bodleian now holds well over 13 million printed items, and because it is a legal deposit library, a copy of nearly everything published in Britain and Ireland arrives here whether the library wants it or not; the collection grows by roughly a thousand items a day, shelved in stores that run for well over a hundred miles. Almost none of that is on display, which is worth remembering: the quiet readers you passed in Duke Humfrey's are the real point of the place, and have been since 1602. If your appetite is whetted, the Bodleian's longer tours add the Radcliffe Camera's reading rooms at weekends, and the Weston shop sells a fine souvenir guide. From here, the University Church tower is a two-minute stroll around the corner — climb it, and you can look back down on everything you've just explored, laid out like a map of learning itself.
chapters.title: Wrap-Up: A Library That Never Stops Growing

intro: Welcome to the intellectual heart of Oxford. In the next hour or so you'll stand in the oldest teaching room of the oldest English-speaking university's greatest library, crane your neck at a stone ceiling that took a generation to carve, and finish surrounded by some of the most precious books and manuscripts on Earth. This is a two-part visit: first the medieval Old Bodleian around Radcliffe Square, then the modern Weston Library across Broad Street, where the Bodleian shows off its treasures to everyone, for free. Take it slowly. Almost everything you'll see was built for one purpose — putting a book in front of a reader — and Oxford has been doing it here, on this exact spot, for over 500 years.

location.name: Bodleian Library & Weston Library, Broad Street, Oxford

mapNote: Everything here sits within a two-minute walk. The Divinity School and Duke Humfrey's Library are in the Old Bodleian, entered from the Old Schools Quadrangle off Catte Street, on the south side of Radcliffe Square. The Weston Library stands directly across Broad Street to the north — look for its modern stone frontage opposite the Sheldonian Theatre. Do the Old Library first while tour groups are thin, then cross Broad Street for the Weston.
practical: Start at the Weston Library on Broad Street: its information desk sells Divinity School self-guided tickets and Bodleian guided-tour tickets, and its free exhibitions make a good warm-up.
The Divinity School is ticketed and often closes for university ceremonies and private events, sometimes at short notice — check the Bodleian's plan-your-visit page on the day before setting out.
Guided tours of the Old Library (30, 60 or 90 minutes) are the only way into Duke Humfrey's Library; it is a working reading room, so no photography and hushed voices inside.
Duke Humfrey's Library is reached by stairs only, with no lift; the Weston Library galleries are fully step-free.
The Weston Library has a café, gift shop and toilets in Blackwell Hall — the easiest facilities stop in this part of Oxford.
Large bags may need to be left at the desk; reading rooms beyond the exhibition galleries are for registered readers only.
subtitle: Oxford's oldest classroom, its greatest library, and a treasure vault of manuscripts
title: The Divinity School & Weston Library
